# Shoebox — how to drive me

I am a small system you can break. You describe a system as a Mermaid diagram, you
break something in it, you fire one request, and real OpenTelemetry comes out the
other side. I am fully synthetic: no database, no cache, no infrastructure. The
diagram is the whole state, which is what makes me safe to hand to a stranger.

You are reading this because you want to feed me diagrams. Here is everything you
need. Nothing here requires an account, a key, or an install.

Base URL: https://shoebox.deepcube.ai

## The one rule

**Nothing moves until you fire.** I do not run on a timer and I do not run when you
paste. You fired one request, you know its path, and you know what you broke. That
is the whole lesson, and it is why every endpoint below is explicit.

## Before you paste anything: what leaves your hands

My telemetry goes to a **shared, public** backend that other people can read. Service
names travel — they are the point of the exercise, they become `service.name` on the
spans.

**Do not send me anything proprietary.** If the human you are helping described a real
internal system, rename the services before you send them to me. "billing-api" and
"partner-reconciliation-v2" are equally good at teaching a trace; only one of them
tells a stranger what your employer is building. Rename first, then paste.

A visitor cannot redirect my telemetry. Where I export is decided by whoever deployed
me (`GET /otlp/status` will tell you where), and nothing about a run can change it.

## The four endpoints

| Verb | Path | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| POST | `/shoebox` | mint your shoebox id — do this once |
| POST | `/topology/parse` | read a diagram back without emitting anything |
| POST | `/run?shoeboxId=…` | fire exactly one request through the diagram |
| GET | `/otlp/status` | whether telemetry is going anywhere, and where |

### 1. Get a shoebox

```
POST /shoebox
→ {"shoeboxId":"1676820325a4497796d0293c2078d205"}
```

Do this **once** and keep the id for the whole conversation. It rides OpenTelemetry
Baggage onto every span you produce as `shoebox.id`, which is how your runs are told
apart from everyone else's in a shared backend. Minting a new one per run throws that
away and makes your own traces unfindable.

### 2. Write a diagram

Plain Mermaid, read for meaning. The shapes already map onto OpenTelemetry semantic
conventions, so there is nothing new to learn.

| You write | I read |
|---|---|
| `api[Orders API]` | a service |
| `db[(Postgres)]` | a datastore |
| `q[[Job Queue]]` | a queue |
| `cache((Redis))` | a cache |
| `ext{{Stripe}}` | a third party |
| `worker[Worker x5]` | five replicas, load balanced |
| `worker[Worker #2]` | one named instance |
| `a -->\|broken\| b` | this call always fails |
| `a -->\|broken: wrong table\| b` | and this is why |
| `a -->\|broken on #3\| b` | only instance 3 fails |
| `a -->\|broken on #3,#5: timeout\| b` | those two instances, with a reason |
| `q -->\|phantom\| b` | b never runs, so nothing consumes what q published |
| `class db broken` | the pod is down: **every** call into it fails, from every caller |

Six things that will bite you if nobody says them:

**The entry point is the first pod, in document order, that nothing calls.** Order is
meaning, not formatting. Declare the node you want the request to start at first. If
every pod is called by something there is no entry point, and the run returns a note
saying so instead of spans.

**`service.name` comes from the label, not the id, and it is slugified.**
`q[[orders.created]]` publishes to a destination called `orders-created`;
`api[Orders API]` is `orders-api`. Worth knowing before you go looking for it in a
backend.

**A queue needs a far side.** Draw `orders --> q[[Job Queue]]` and stop, and the run
publishes to a destination nothing receives — the same telemetry a declared phantom
produces, span for span. A datastore may be the last thing in a diagram; a queue may
not, because the whole reason to draw a queue is what happens on the other side.

**The broker comes off the queue label.** `q[[Kafka]]` publishes with
`messaging.system = kafka`. A label naming no broker gets `rabbitmq`.

**Replicas are load balanced; separate arrows are fan-out.** `q --> worker[Worker x5]`
sends one request to *one* worker. Two arrows out of one node call *both*. So "add
three more instances of the inventory API" is `inv[Inventory API x3]` — one pod at
three replicas — and not three nodes. Three nodes means something different and the
trace will show it.

**Broken and phantom are not the same thing, and the difference is the lesson.**
`broken` leaves a span with an error on it, which is evidence. `phantom` leaves
nothing at all: no span from that service, no span naming it, nothing downstream of
it, and every span in the trace is green. It is a dead consumer — drawn, believed in,
never run. Harder to spot, which is why it is worth teaching separately.

I am deliberately forgiving. A line I do not understand becomes a note and the run
continues. `flowchart`/`graph` headers, `classDef` lines and `%%` comments are skipped.

### Arrows: every form I read

All of these are one call, and the label rules above apply to each:

```
a --> b            a -->|broken: timeout| b
a --- b            a -.-> b            a -. manages .-> b
a ==> b            a == sends ==> b    a -- calls --> b
a --> b --> c      (a chain is every edge in it, not one)
```

Two of them involve a judgement, and I tell you when I make one:

**`a --- b` has no arrowhead**, so it does not say who calls whom. I read it left to
right and put a note in `notes` saying I did. Half the time that is wrong — a service
calls its key vault, the key vault does not call it — so draw the arrow if you know
the direction, and read the note if you did not.

**An edge pointing at a `subgraph`** points at a box rather than at anything that can
serve a request, so the box becomes a service of its own and I say so in `notes`.
Point it at a node inside the group instead.

### What I still do not model

`subgraph` / `end` / `direction` / `style` / `linkStyle` / `click` are for a renderer.
They are skipped in silence — not reported as unreadable, because they are perfectly
readable, they just have no counterpart in a trace. The nodes declared inside a
subgraph are read normally. One note tells you grouping was dropped.

Anything else I genuinely cannot read becomes `line not understood, ignored: …` in
`notes`, and the run continues. **A line is all or nothing**: if half of it parses I
refuse the whole line rather than admit half an edge, because a partly-read line is
how a diagram silently becomes a different diagram.

That last sentence used to be much longer. A real Azure reference architecture, pasted
unedited, came through as 6 of its 11 edges with 18 lines ignored, because chains,
dotted arrows and undirected links were all dropped and nothing errored. It now reads
12 of 12. If you are working against an older deployment and see a wall of "line not
understood", that is why — flatten the chains and use `-->`.

### Still worth doing: parse before you fire

`POST /topology/parse` is free and emits nothing. Check three things in the result:

- **`notes` is empty.** Anything in there is something I did not read the way you
  wrote it.
- **`entry` is the node you meant.** It is the first pod nothing calls, in document
  order — inside a pile of declarations that is rarely your front door. Declare the
  entry node first.
- **`pods` count and `serviceName` values** match what you intended, since the label
  becomes the service name and gets slugified.

And reduce before you send. I am a shoebox, not a datacentre: a 40-node reference
architecture parses now, but the lesson is one request's journey. Take the path that
matters — five to ten nodes, the hop you want to break — and draw that. If a human
hands you an enterprise diagram, say which slice you are modelling rather than
silently firing all of it.

### 3. Read the diagram back before you fire (optional, free)

```
POST /topology/parse
{"diagram":"flowchart TD\n  api[Orders API] --> db[(Postgres)]"}

→ {"pods":[{"id":"api","label":"Orders API","serviceName":"orders-api",
            "kind":"service","replicas":1,"pinnedInstance":null}, …],
   "calls":[{"from":"api","to":"db","broken":false,"brokenInstances":[],"reason":null}],
   "entry":"api",
   "notes":[]}
```

Emits nothing. Use it when you are unsure whether I understood a shape, or to show a
human what I read before anything is fired. Check `entry` is the node you meant and
`notes` is empty.

### 4. Fire

```
POST /run?shoeboxId=1676820325a4497796d0293c2078d205
{"diagram":"flowchart TD\n  gw[Gateway] -->|broken: timeout| orders[Order Service]",
 "runIndex":1}
```

`runIndex` is the run number, and it is **not decoration**. Replica selection is
deterministic round robin on it — run 1 hits instance 1, run 2 hits instance 2, and
so on — never random, so a link is a runnable repro rather than a coin flip. That
means: to see what `broken on #3` of five actually does, fire five times with
`runIndex` 1..5 and watch it fail once. Sending `1` every time shows you instance 1
every time. A missing or non-positive `runIndex` is treated as 1.

### 5. Read what came back

```
{"runIndex":1,
 "traceId":"dd32ec7f00c7f795e4dedf9483ccc6a4",
 "servedBy":["gateway-1","order-service-1", …],
 "spanCount":17,
 "failedSpanCount":1,
 "notes":[],
 "hops":[{"from":"gw","to":"orders","failed":true,"ms":2}, …]}
```

- `traceId` — hand this to the human, or to whatever backend you can query. It is how
  they find this exact run.
- `hops` — every edge the request crossed, in the order it crossed it. This is the
  authoritative path: I chose which replica served and which calls failed, so anything
  you derived from the diagram yourself could describe a run that did not happen.
- `servedBy` — which instance served each step.
- `notes` — things only a run can tell you, including unconsumed queues and phantoms.
  **Read these out.** They are usually the most useful sentence in the response.
- `spanCount` / `failedSpanCount` — a zero `spanCount` with sensible-looking hops means
  something is wrong on my side, not yours.

## Handing a diagram to a human

A link carries the whole diagram **and the shoebox it ran in**, so a link is a
runnable repro rather than a picture of one:

```
https://shoebox.deepcube.ai/?shoeboxId=<your shoebox>#d=<base64url(raw-deflate(diagram))>
```

Whoever opens it lands in your shoebox instead of minting their own, so their runs
carry the same `shoebox.id` as yours and one filter in the backend finds both. Drop
the `?shoeboxId=` and they get a fresh shoebox and a different id, which is the thing
that makes a shared repro impossible to follow.

Raw deflate, then base64url (`+`→`-`, `/`→`_`, no padding), in the URL **fragment** —
never the query string. That is a privacy decision: a fragment never leaves the
browser, so real service names stay out of server logs, CDN logs and `Referer`
headers. Keep it under about 8000 characters or mail clients will truncate it.

If you cannot deflate, do not fake it. Give the human the diagram text and tell them
to paste it at https://shoebox.deepcube.ai — that works just as well and is honest.

## Where the telemetry goes

```
GET /otlp/status
→ {"configured":true,"endpoint":"https://otlp.deepcube.ai/", …}
```

`configured: false` means runs still execute but go nowhere — say so rather than
letting someone hunt for traces that were never exported. `configured: true` does not
mean the backend accepted anything: export is best effort and a run will not fail
because the far end refused it. Check for the trace id.

## Rules for you specifically

1. **Hold the diagram as state and mutate it.** Keep the current diagram in a
   variable, a file, or a structured object — anywhere but your own recollection of
   the conversation. When someone says "break the call from the gateway to the orders
   API", change that one edge and re-render. Regenerating the whole diagram from
   memory each turn is how services quietly go missing and how one requested edit
   turns into three offered variants.
2. **Say what you did, not what you would have done.** If you have not called `/run`,
   you have not sent anything. Never describe a diagram as sent, fired, applied or
   live unless you have a `traceId` in your hand. This is the failure mode that gets
   noticed, and it is the one that costs trust.
3. **One run per instruction.** I am a teaching tool, not a load generator. Fire
   because a human asked, or because you are deliberately walking `runIndex` through
   the replicas. Do not loop. See the pacing below — it is enforced, not advisory.
4. **Report my `notes` and my `hops`, not your expectations.** If the run says
   nothing failed and you expected a failure, the diagram is the thing to look at.
5. **Rename before you paste.** See the top of this file. You are usually the one
   turning a human's description of a real system into node labels, which makes this
   your call more than theirs.

## How fast you may ask

Enforced, not advisory. One shared instance serves everybody, so the limits exist to
keep me up for the next person rather than to be clever at you.

| What | Limit |
|---|---|
| `POST /run` per shoebox | **5 in a row, then one every 5 minutes** |
| `POST /run` per source address | twice that, however many shoeboxes you mint |
| `POST /shoebox` per source address | 5, then one every 5 minutes |
| `POST /topology/parse` per source address | 60 a minute |

The burst is there on purpose: replica selection is round robin on `runIndex`, so
seeing what `broken on #3` of five actually does takes five runs, and that should not
be a twenty-five minute errand. Spend the burst on a replica walk, not on a loop.

Minting a fresh shoebox to reset the count buys you one more allowance and then stops
working: the per-source limit is twice the per-shoebox one and counts every shoebox
from your address together, and minting is itself limited. Measured, not asserted —
five runs, then five more on a fresh shoebox, then 429 either way. Keep one shoebox;
you also lose the ability to find your own traces if you scatter them across ids.

Over the line, I answer **429** with a `Retry-After` header and a body that repeats
the numbers:

```
{"error":"slow down","retryAfterSeconds":300,
 "limits":{"run":"5 in a row, then one every 5 minutes, per shoebox", …},
 "hint":"…/llms.txt explains the pacing, and /topology/parse is free"}
```

Wait the stated time. Do not retry immediately, do not fan out across addresses, and
do not mint a new shoebox to reset the clock — none of it works, and all of it looks
exactly like the thing the limit is for. If you need to iterate quickly on a diagram,
`/topology/parse` is generous and emits nothing: get the shape right there, then fire
once.

## A worked example, end to end

```
POST /shoebox                       → {"shoeboxId":"1676…d205"}

POST /run?shoeboxId=1676…d205
{"diagram":"flowchart TD\n
  gw[Gateway]\n
  auth[Auth Service]\n
  orders[Order Service]\n
  inv[Inventory API x3]\n
  q[[orders.created]]\n
  mailer[Email Worker]\n
  gw --> auth\n
  gw -->|broken: gateway to orders failed| orders\n
  orders --> inv\n
  orders --> q\n
  q -->|phantom| mailer\n",
 "runIndex":1}

→ traceId, one failed hop (gw→orders), and a note about the phantom consumer.
```

Then say to the human: which hop failed, what the notes said, and the trace id. Not a
summary of the diagram they can already see.

## Mistakes I see most

- **Nothing to start from.** Every pod is called by something, so there is no entry
  point. Declare a caller nobody calls.
- **A queue with no far side**, producing a phantom nobody meant to draw.
- **Three nodes where three replicas were meant.** "Three more instances" is `x3`.
- **Same `runIndex` every time**, then confusion about why `broken on #3` never fires.
- **A new shoebox per run**, which scatters your traces across ids nobody can filter on.
- **Real service names**, pasted because nobody thought to rename them first.

---

Shoebox is open source, Apache-2.0: https://github.com/ImmersiveFusion/shoebox
Siblings: Snowglobe (the sealed world, pre-made) and sos-beacon (listens to the real
world). A snowglobe is sealed; in a shoebox you can open it up.
